newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canadian reporting standards under fire over Bre-X.
newsitem.headline: Canadian reporting standards under fire over Bre-X.

text.p: Australian mining industry officials believe the Busang gold controversy which is rocking stock exchanges is likely to bring maverick Canada into line with mineral reporting standards adopted by leading mining countries in the Western world.

Norman Miskelly, head of an Australian mining industry reporting standards committee, told Reuters the Toronto-listed Bre-X Minerals Ltd situation could "not really" have occurred if Canada had adopted mining reporting standards which it has been under pressure to take up for years.
"Well, I guess it could have (happened) but it would not have lasted so long," he added.
Britain, the United States and South Africa were now in line with Australian standards. "The difficulty has been Canada," Miskelly said.

After Canada joined other leading Western mining nations in 1994 to use the Australian disclosure model as a starting point for new regulations, standards in those countries became "85 percent the same", Miskelly said.
"But its like an aeroplane going into international air space. You've got to make sure its 100 percent the same."

Miskelly is chairman of the Joint Ore Reserves Committee, which comprises six organisations including the Australian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy and the Minerals Council of Australia. He is also convenor of the London-based Council of Mining and Metallurgy Institutions, an umbrella body for principal mining institutes.
Canada was the only country "dragging its feet" in efforts to have the U.S., Australia, South Africa, Britain and Canada adopt the same reporting code, Miskelly said.

It was not that Canada saw gain for itself in becoming a listing heaven for mining groups, but rather that internal fragmentation in Canada stood in the way of agreement, he said. Canada has five different stock exchanges, a number of provincial securities commissions and several engineering associations.
"They're all going in different directions. It's like Australia was 30 years ago," he said.

"Canada (also) does not have ... effective ethical standards in terms of if somebody does something wrong or potentially misleading or fraudulent they can't take the licence to operate away from that particular person," he said.
"The back-up of an ethical inquiry is a very powerful influence in terms of keeping people honest.
"I would suggest the Bre-X thing will cause them to address this with great dedication they have not had before," he said.
Miskelly said invitations in the wake of the Bre-X controversy for him to present his views in Canada could help break the gridlock.
"I see this as very positive in terms of a ... quick resolution (Canadian agreement)," Miskelly told Reuters.

Direct approaches are unlikely to be made to Canadian stock exchanges by the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) for them to adopt Australian reporting standards. But Miskelly's views are backed by the ASX, which adopted the Joint Ore reserves code in its listing rules in 1989.

Agreement was required on only seven definitions for Canada to come into line, Miskelly said. These were on resources, reserves, measured resources, indicated resources, inferred resources, proven reserves and probable reserves and could be
set out on as few as two pages, he said.

"I would like to think that by the end of the year we will have resolved the outstanding differences in the definitions (and)...have reached substantive if not complete agreement on a standard definition in these areas," Miskelly said.

Bre-X faces seven class action lawsuits after its shares collapsed following assay reports by its partner in Busang Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc which severely discounted earlier statements that the deposit contains 70.95 million ounces of gold, the biggest in the world.
